subtype: Loud reactions online and voice notes [Mismatch]
passage: In the open-plan office of the ad agency, Jatin's screen lit up with a message from Ramesh: "WE GOT THE CLIENT!!!" Jatin grinned, because Ramesh always typed in capitals when thrilled. Ten minutes later the same manager pinged the whole team: "WHY IS THE FILE STILL NOT SENT???" Jatin's stomach dropped. Was that anger or panic? Nobody in the room could tell. Ramesh, at the next desk, caught Jatin's eye and said, "Should we ask her what she needs?" They walked over. It turned out she was terrified the client would leave and needed the file in an hour. Jatin sent it in twenty minutes and exhaled.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's first message say?
qa.a: Ramesh's message said "WE GOT THE CLIENT!!!"

qa.q: What did Jatin feel when the manager's capitals arrived, and what did they turn out to mean?
qa.a: Jatin's stomach dropped and Jatin could not tell if the capitals meant anger or panic. It turned out the manager was terrified of losing the client.

qa.q: What helped clear up the tone of the message?
qa.a: Ramesh suggested asking the manager what was needed, and a short walk over cleared it up.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt when the team seemed to hesitate?
qa.a: The manager was probably stressed and rushed and may not have noticed how the capitals sounded to others.

grounding: Illustrates ALL CAPS and many exclamation marks read as either excitement or anger, cleared up by asking directly.

subtype: Loud reactions online and voice notes [Mismatch]
passage:
Dear Nandini,

I got your voice note yesterday and, honestly, I thought you were furious. You were loud, fast, and your voice cracked on "how could you". I nearly wrote back angrily. Then I remembered that you shout when you are excited, and you had also just come from the match. So I called instead, and it turned out you were thrilled about the office move and wanted to tell me all at once! I laughed. I was so relieved I did not fire off a nasty reply. Next time I will ask before assuming, and please tell me when you are only excited. 🙂

Farida

qa.q: What did Farida do instead of writing back angrily?
qa.a: Farida called Nandini instead.

qa.q: What did Farida first think of Nandini's loud voice note, and what was the truth?
qa.a: Farida thought Nandini was furious, but Nandini was actually thrilled about the office move. Loud and fast voices can carry excitement or anger, so Farida checked.

qa.q: What did Farida do that avoided a quarrel?
qa.a: Farida called and asked instead of replying angrily, and offered to ask before assuming next time.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt on hearing Farida had thought that?
qa.a: Nandini might have felt surprised and a bit sorry, having only meant to share excitement.

grounding: Letter about a loud, fast voice note read as anger but meant as excitement, cleared up by a quick call.

subtype: Screaming and public safety [Interpreting]
passage: Counsellor's note, Tuesday. I am Sharmila, hostel counsellor. Last night a student, Minakshi, told me she heard a loud scream from the lane behind the hostel around ten. She froze at the window, unsure whether it was friends playing, a film on someone's phone or trouble. She wanted to run down. I said that rushing in alone would not be wise. Instead she called the warden, who sent the security guard. It turned out a stray dog had bitten someone's bag and a girl had shrieked in fright. Nobody was hurt. Minakshi said her heart raced for an hour. I praised her for calling and not going alone, and I will check on her this week.

qa.q: Who did Minakshi call?
qa.a: Minakshi called the warden.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling at the window, and what does the racing heart suggest?
qa.a: Minakshi was frightened and unsure whether it was play or danger, and wanted to rush out. The racing heart suggests she took the scream seriously and it stayed with her.

qa.q: What was the safer choice than running into the lane?
qa.a: Calling the warden so the security guard could go was safer than rushing in alone.

qa.q: How might the girl who shrieked have felt afterwards?
qa.a: She had been frightened by the dog, so she may have felt startled and shaken, and possibly embarrassed that it caused alarm.

grounding: Counsellor's note on a young adult hearing a scream and choosing to call the warden and guard instead of ignoring it or rushing in alone.

subtype: Screaming and public safety [Interpreting]
passage:
Sat. 11:15 pm. Heard a scream from the street below the flat. Maria and I froze mid-chat. My first thought was a horror film someone was streaming. Then it came again, higher, and a voice shouting "Leave me alone!" My legs wanted to run downstairs. Maria held my arm and said, "Do not go alone." We called the emergency number and told them the address and what we heard. Then we watched from the window. Two neighbours came out and a police vehicle arrived. It was a quarrel that got out of hand. Nobody was badly hurt. I am still shaky, but I am glad we called.
- Simran

qa.q: What did Simran and Maria do after the second scream?
qa.a: They called the emergency number and gave the address and what they heard.

qa.q: What did Simran feel when the scream came again, and how do you know?
qa.a: Simran felt alarmed and wanted to run downstairs, and the first guess of a film gave way to worry once the words "Leave me alone!" were heard.

qa.q: Which choice was wise, and why?
qa.a: Calling the emergency number instead of going down alone was wise, because trained people could reach the street safely.

qa.q: How might Maria have felt when Simran wanted to run down?
qa.a: Maria was probably worried about Simran's safety, which is why Maria held the arm and said not to go alone.

grounding: Diary entry about hearing a scream, weighing play, film or danger, and calling emergency help instead of ignoring or rushing in alone.

subtype: Groaning, moaning and pain [Interpreting]
passage: I sit across from Jaya in the maths department, and for two days I heard groans from her side of the room. Everyone joked. "Monday blues," said the professor. Jaya laughed too, but then leaned on the desk with her hand at her side and let out a low moan she did not seem to notice. I did not know whether it was theatre, tiredness or real pain. I am Uma, and I decided not to assume. I went over and asked quietly, "Are you all right? Should I get someone?" Jaya said her side had hurt since the morning. We told the department head and she went to the doctor.

qa.q: Where did Uma sit compared with Jaya?
qa.a: Uma sits across from Jaya in the maths department.

qa.q: What did Uma think of Jaya's groans, and why did Uma ask?
qa.a: Uma could not tell whether the groans were joking, tiredness or real pain, and chose to ask instead of assuming. A quiet moan Jaya did not seem to notice made Uma more concerned.

qa.q: What was a wise thing Uma did?
qa.a: Uma asked quietly and offered to get someone, then helped tell the department head so Jaya could see a doctor.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt when everyone joked about the Monday blues?
qa.a: Jaya may have felt embarrassed to speak up about real pain, since Jaya laughed along at first.

grounding: Observer's account of a young adult hearing groans and moans and asking and helping instead of assuming exaggeration.

subtype: Groaning, moaning and pain [Interpreting]
passage:
Day 1. Yogesh groaned loudly as he stood up from his desk and Dhruv joked, "Getting old, boss." Yogesh laughed but rubbed his back.

Day 3. The groans got deeper when Yogesh stood, and once he stopped with a hand on the wall, breathing carefully. Dhruv noticed the change and quietly asked, "That does not sound like a joke. Is it hurting?" Yogesh admitted it had been bad for days.

Day 4. Dhruv walked with Yogesh to the clinic and sat with him in the waiting room. "Let the doctor look at it," he said. Yogesh nodded, relieved that someone had believed him.

qa.q: Who went with Yogesh to the clinic?
qa.a: Dhruv walked with Yogesh to the clinic.

qa.q: What made Dhruv change from joking to asking about the groans?
qa.a: The groans got deeper and Yogesh stopped with a hand on the wall, breathing carefully, so it no longer sounded like a joke. It could still have been tiredness, so Dhruv asked.

qa.q: What did Dhruv do that helped?
qa.a: Dhruv asked kindly, went to the clinic with Yogesh and suggested letting the doctor look at it.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt when first teased?
qa.a: Yogesh probably felt brushed off, since Yogesh laughed but kept rubbing the back, and later felt relieved to be believed.

grounding: Before, during and after account of groans that Dhruv first jokes about and then, noticing the change, asks about and helps with.

subtype: Throat-clearing and grunts in meetings [Interpreting]
passage: Note from the team lead, Thursday. I am Zainab. In the design meeting, Aditi cleared her throat sharply twice while Manav presented, and the room went stiff. Some thought she disagreed and Manav looked worried. I thought it could also be a tickle. I decided not to guess, so at the end I said, "Aditi, is there anything you would like to say on that?" She said she had a dry throat and had been meaning to mention a small point about the colour palette. Manav laughed with relief. I noted that a throat-clear is a weak cue and that a simple follow-up question worked well. I will encourage direct follow-ups.

qa.q: What did Aditi mention at the end?
qa.a: She mentioned a small point about the colour palette.

qa.q: What did Manav think when Aditi cleared her throat, and what was the truth?
qa.a: Manav looked worried, as if it meant disagreement. The truth was that Aditi had a dry throat and a small point to add.

qa.q: What worked in Zainab's approach?
qa.a: Zainab asked, "Aditi, is there anything you would like to say on that?" instead of guessing at the meaning.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt when the room went stiff?
qa.a: Aditi may have been unaware or embarrassed, since a dry throat was all it was.

grounding: Team lead's note on a throat-clear that colleagues read as disagreement, resolved by a simple follow-up question.

subtype: Throat-clearing and grunts in meetings [Interpreting]
passage: Wed, 8 pm. In today's client call, Shreya grunted when Manjula said the launch might slip. I am Manjula, and my chest tightened. Did the grunt mean she disagreed? Was she annoyed? I wanted to ask but felt shy. During the second half, Shreya cleared her throat again while I talked and I lost my place. After the call I sent a message: "Is there a point you would like to raise about the launch date?" Shreya replied, "Sorry, I have a cold and was clearing my throat. But yes, I had one thought." We spoke for five minutes. I need to remember these sounds are weak cues. Asking is fairer than guessing.

qa.q: What did Shreya say she had?
qa.a: Shreya said she had a cold.

qa.q: What did Manjula think when Shreya grunted, and what was going on?
qa.a: Manjula's chest tightened as if the grunt might mean disagreement or annoyance. In fact Shreya had a cold and one thought to add.

qa.q: What did Manjula do that helped?
qa.a: Manjula sent a message asking whether Shreya had a point to raise about the launch date.

qa.q: How might Shreya have seen the exchange?
qa.a: Shreya probably had no idea the throat sounds had worried Manjula, and was glad of the chance to share the thought.

grounding: Diary entry about a throat-clear or grunt read as possible disagreement, resolved by a follow-up question.

subtype: Oops, ouch and apologetic sounds at work [Expressing]
passage:
Week 1. Pankaj dropped a tray of samples at the lab and said, "Oops!" with a small laugh. Uma, the lab head, smiled and helped pick them up. It lightened the moment.

Week 3. Pankaj mislabelled a batch and said, "Oops," and moved on. Uma said, "That one matters. Let us recheck the labels together." Pankaj went red, then said, "Sorry, that was a serious mistake. I will fix it today."

Week 5. A colleague's remark stung and Pankaj said "Ouch" softly. The colleague smiled and said, "Fair, I was blunt." Pankaj felt understood.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say after mislabelling a batch?
qa.a: Pankaj said, "Oops," and moved on.

qa.q: What did Pankaj feel when Uma said the mistake mattered, and how do you know?
qa.a: Pankaj felt embarrassed and realised the mistake was serious, shown by going red and saying "Sorry, that was a serious mistake." The "oops" had been too light for it.

qa.q: What is a better response than "oops" alone for a mistake that mattered?
qa.a: A proper apology and a concrete fix, as Pankaj gave by promising to correct the labels that day.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt when Pankaj said "Oops" about the labels?
qa.a: Uma may have felt concerned that the mistake was being brushed off, which is why Uma said it mattered.

grounding: Illustrates small sounds like oops and ouch that lighten a moment but do not replace a proper apology when the mistake mattered.

subtype: Oops, ouch and apologetic sounds at work [Expressing]
passage: When I was a junior in the print office, Arnab, I said "oops" for everything. Elder here, Kalyani. I once dropped a stack of forms and giggled, "Oops!" and my senior smiled. Good. It lightened the moment. Later I sent the wrong invoice to a client and, again, said "oops" and walked away. My senior called me back gently and said, "That is not an oops. Fix it and tell them." I felt my face burn. I wrote an apology and phoned the client. Small sounds are fine, Arnab, they show you are human. But when the mistake costs someone, say sorry properly and mend it. The word oops is only the start.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say when dropping a stack of forms?
qa.a: Kalyani giggled and said, "Oops!"

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the senior said "That is not an oops"?
qa.a: Kalyani felt embarrassment, shown by the burning face, and realised the invoice mistake needed more than a light sound.

qa.q: What lesson does Kalyani give to Arnab about small sounds?
qa.a: Small sounds are fine for light slips, but when a mistake costs someone, apologise properly and fix it.

qa.q: How might the client have felt about the wrong invoice?
qa.a: The client was probably confused or inconvenienced, and would appreciate a real apology and a phone call.

grounding: Elder's story about saying oops after errors, which lightens minor moments but should not replace a proper apology or fix when the mistake mattered.

subtype: Um, uh and filler in public speaking [Regulating]
passage: The conference hall was full and the projector hummed. Salma stepped up to give her first presentation on library funding. Her hands were damp, and she said, "Um, so, uh, thank you all for coming." She heard herself and stopped. Elizabeth, her mentor, in the front row, had told her once: pause instead. So Salma paused, breathed, looked at her notes and said, "Today I will share three findings." The room was quiet and attentive. The silence felt long to her, though probably only a moment. Later Elizabeth said, "Nobody noticed the um at the start. But the pause made you sound sure."

qa.q: What was Salma's presentation about?
qa.a: It was about library funding.

qa.q: How did Salma feel at the start of the talk, and what evidence suggests it?
qa.a: Salma was nervous, shown by her damp hands and the "um, so, uh" opening. The pause helped her steady herself.

qa.q: What could Salma try in her next talk?
qa.a: Salma could keep pausing and breathing instead of filling the gap with um and uh, as Elizabeth suggested.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have felt watching Salma pause?
qa.a: Elizabeth probably felt proud and reassured, since the pause made Salma sound sure.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional replacing um and uh with a pause during a presentation, which reads as more confident.

subtype: Um, uh and filler in public speaking [Regulating]
passage:
Dear Akash,

Thank you for coming to my talk, and for the feedback afterwards. You said I said "um" eleven times in the first minute, and I laughed, but it made me think. I practised at home with my phone recording and tried to replace each um with a short silence. It felt strange and long at first, as if the whole room would notice. But when I watched the video, the pause looked calm and thoughtful. I also learned that fillers do not mean I do not know my subject; I do, I was just nervous. I will try the pause at the department seminar next week. 🙂

Aparna

qa.q: What did Aparna practise with at home?
qa.a: Aparna practised with a phone recording.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when the pause first felt long, and what did the video show?
qa.a: Aparna felt the silence was strange and long and worried the room would notice. The video showed the pause looked calm and thoughtful.

qa.q: What could Aparna do at the department seminar?
qa.a: Aparna could replace ums with short pauses and breaths, as practised.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt giving that feedback?
qa.a: Akash probably wanted to help and hoped Aparna would take it kindly, since the count was given as feedback and Aparna laughed.

grounding: Letter from a young professional who practises replacing um and uh with a pause while presenting.

subtype: Cultural norms about volume and pitch [Mismatch]
passage: Cross-cultural onboarding note. I am Kunal, and I supervise the Lagos and Pune teams. In Monday's call, Samir spoke softly and slowly to the group, and Nilesh from Lagos took it as shyness. Later, Nilesh spoke loudly and warmly, laughing, and Samir stiffened, thinking Nilesh was angry. I explained privately to each of them: in Pune, soft speech often means respect; in Nilesh's team, a loud, warm voice means friendliness. Neither was a fault of character. On Wednesday Samir said, "Nilesh, your energy helps me," and Nilesh said, "Samir, your calm helps me." I will keep watching for misunderstandings.

qa.q: Which two teams does Kunal supervise?
qa.a: Kunal supervises the Lagos and Pune teams.

qa.q: What did Samir think when Nilesh spoke loudly, and what did Nilesh mean?
qa.a: Samir stiffened and thought Nilesh was angry, but Nilesh meant to be friendly and warm. Volume alone did not show which.

qa.q: What helped the two work together?
qa.a: Kunal explained the different norms privately to each, and they began to name what helped them about each other.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have felt when Samir's soft speech seemed to signal shyness?
qa.a: Nilesh may have felt uncertain how to connect, since Nilesh's warmth was met with quiet and might have seemed to be unwelcome.

grounding: Supervisor's note on cross-cultural differences in loud or soft speech, showing volume alone should not be used to judge character.

subtype: Cultural norms about volume and pitch [Mismatch]
passage: Tue night. Nilesh here, diary. Three weeks on the Zurich team and I am still confused about volume. At home in Kolkata, we talk loudly and over each other, and it means we like you. Here, when I told a joke loudly, the room went quiet, and I could feel people stiffening. Tarun, the quiet one, said later, "People think you are upset when you raise your voice." I was shocked. I was happy! Then I saw that Tarun's soft voice, which I took as boredom, is his way of being polite. Neither of us is wrong. I am going to lower my volume a bit and ask Tarun about his day.

qa.q: Where does Nilesh work now?
qa.a: Nilesh works on the Zurich team.

qa.q: What did Nilesh feel when Tarun said people think he is upset, and what was the truth?
qa.a: Nilesh was shocked, since the loud voice meant happiness and warmth at home in Kolkata. In Zurich it read as being upset.

qa.q: What is Nilesh going to try?
qa.a: Nilesh plans to lower the volume a bit and ask Tarun about his day.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt when Nilesh joked loudly?
qa.a: Tarun may have felt uneasy, since loud talk can seem like upset or aggression in that setting, though Tarun spoke kindly afterwards.

grounding: Diary entry about a young professional finding that loud talk signals friendliness in one place and upset in another, and soft speech may be politeness.

subtype: Lowering the voice to de-escalate [Regulating]
passage: At the small hardware shop in the kasba, an angry customer slapped a broken pump on the counter. "You sold me rubbish! I want my money back!" Sachin's cheeks burned and he wanted to shout back. But Chandrika, the owner's niece, stepped forward and lowered her voice. "Uncle, please sit. Tell me what happened, slowly." The customer, still red, said the pump had stopped after two days. "That sounds frustrating," Chandrika said, steady and soft. "Let me check it with you." The man's shoulders came down. Sachin watched, ashamed of his first urge. The customer left with a replacement, still grumbling but calmer.

qa.q: What did the angry customer put on the counter?
qa.a: He slapped a broken pump on the counter.

qa.q: What did Sachin feel when the customer shouted, and how did Chandrika's tone change things?
qa.a: Sachin felt angry and wanted to shout back, but Chandrika's low, slow voice let the customer's shoulders come down. Matching the anger could have made it worse.

qa.q: What could Sachin learn from Chandrika?
qa.a: Sachin can speak slower, lower and softer, and ask the customer to explain, rather than match the anger.

qa.q: How might the customer have felt when Chandrika lowered her voice?
qa.a: The customer probably felt heard and less defensive, since the shoulders came down.

grounding: Rural narrative of a young adult lowering the voice and slowing down to calm an angry customer instead of matching the anger.

subtype: Lowering the voice to de-escalate [Regulating]
passage: The delivery driver came into the cafe in Lagos shouting that his parcel was missing and demanding to speak to the manager. Yara, the barista, felt her pulse jump. Her first thought was to answer sharply. Instead she put down the cups, slowed her breathing and said, in a low, even voice, "I hear you. Let us find out where it went." Nkechi, the manager, came over and did the same. The driver's voice dropped a little. They checked the storeroom together and found the parcel under a chair. He apologised, embarrassed. Yara said nothing more than, "No problem," and went back to her cups. Had he threatened them, she would have called security.

qa.q: Where was the missing parcel found?
qa.a: It was found under a chair.

qa.q: What did Yara feel when the driver shouted, and what did she do about it?
qa.a: Yara felt her pulse jump and first wanted to answer sharply, but she slowed her breathing and spoke low and even. A steady tone showed control and care.

qa.q: When would leaving or calling security be right?
qa.a: If the driver had threatened them, Yara would have called security, since calm speech is not a guarantee of safety.

qa.q: How might the driver have felt on finding the parcel?
qa.a: He was embarrassed, since he apologised after the shouting.

grounding: Third-person narrative set abroad of a young adult using a slower, lower voice to calm an angry customer, with leaving or security if threats appear.

subtype: Harsh voice at work and de-escalation [Interpreting]
passage: In the bank branch, the manager's phone rang and a client's rough, strained voice filled the room: "I have been waiting three days for my statement!" Simran, the junior officer, felt her own voice rise to match. Then she recalled what Rekha, her mentor, had said: a raspy, tight voice means the person is very worked up. So Simran lowered her volume, slowed down and said, "I understand you have waited a long time, and I am sorry. Let me look at it now." The client took a breath. "Thank you," he said, hoarse and quieter. Simran found the statement in ten minutes and emailed it while he waited.

qa.q: How long had the client waited for the statement?
qa.a: The client said he had waited three days.

qa.q: What did Simran feel first, and what helped her change course?
qa.a: Simran felt her own voice rise to match the anger, but she remembered that a strained voice shows high arousal. She then lowered her volume and acknowledged the client's wait.

qa.q: What would you advise a new officer facing a harsh, strained voice?
qa.a: Lower the volume, slow down and acknowledge the concern, as Simran did, before fixing the problem.

qa.q: How might the client have felt after Simran apologised?
qa.a: The client probably felt heard and calmer, since he took a breath and thanked Simran in a quieter voice.

grounding: Institutional scene of a harsh or strained voice read as high arousal and calmed by lowering own volume, slowing down and acknowledging the concern.

subtype: Harsh voice at work and de-escalation [Interpreting]
passage:
Dear Mohit,

I wanted to write about Tuesday's call with the supplier. His voice was harsh and raspy, and he was shouting about a late delivery. My first instinct was to snap back. Instead I remembered what we discussed after the training: a strained voice like that usually means the person is very worked up, not that they are attacking me. So I lowered my own voice, slowed down and said, "I hear that this delay has cost you. Tell me what you need." His voice softened a little after that. We agreed a new date. I would like your view on whether I should have offered more at the start. 🙂

Divyansh

qa.q: What was the supplier shouting about?
qa.a: The supplier was shouting about a late delivery.

qa.q: What did Divyansh want to do at first, and what did Divyansh decide instead?
qa.a: Divyansh wanted to snap back but remembered that a harsh, strained voice shows the person is worked up. Divyansh chose to lower the voice and acknowledge the cost of the delay.

qa.q: What could Divyansh consider offering earlier next time?
qa.a: Divyansh could acknowledge the concern and ask what is needed right at the start, as the letter wonders.

qa.q: How might the supplier have felt when Divyansh spoke calmly?
qa.a: The supplier probably felt heard, since the voice softened and a new date was agreed.

grounding: Letter about a harsh, strained voice from an angry supplier treated as high arousal and calmed by lowering own volume, slowing down and acknowledging.

subtype: Voice on calls and voice notes [Mismatch]
passage:

subtype: Voice on calls and voice notes [Mismatch]
passage: Elder here, Sharmila. Mahima, you asked why I ring instead of relying on voice notes. Let me tell you. Years ago, my colleague's voice on the phone sounded flat, breathy and very tired. I decided she was sulking and I was cold to her for a week. Then I met her and she was cheerful. The line had been bad and her phone was old. Voices on the phone lose so much: the face, the small smile, everything. Now if someone sounds tired or short, I do not decide. I say, "You sound a bit low, is it the line or is something on your mind?" It costs nothing and saves me from foolish weeks.

qa.q: How long was Sharmila cold to the colleague?
qa.a: Sharmila was cold for a week.

qa.q: What was Sharmila thinking about the colleague's flat voice at first, and what was the truth?
qa.a: Sharmila decided the colleague was sulking, but the flat voice came from a bad line and an old phone. Phone voices lose the face and small smile.

qa.q: What does Sharmila say now when someone sounds low on the phone?
qa.a: Sharmila asks whether it is the line or something on the person's mind, instead of deciding.

qa.q: How might the colleague have felt when Sharmila was cold for a week?
qa.a: The colleague was probably confused or hurt without knowing why, since the cause was only a bad line.

grounding: Elder's story about a flat or breathy voice on a phone line that may be a poor connection, where checking in beats guessing.
